name: Sajolang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.

tone_statements.citation: Blench, Roger. 2018. Mijiic, the Miji and Bangru languages: distribution, dialects, wordlist and classification. Manuscript, Cambridge (rogerblench.info); earlier version 2015 'The Mijiic languages'.
tone_statements.quote: 2.1.3 Tones. Weedall (2013) does not find tone to be contrastive. At a phonetic level, Miji has a simple tonal system, with two tones, High (H ˊ) and Low (L ˋ). Whether these are predictable and related to syllables with a glottal coda, remains to be resolved. Phonetic glide tones are heard on VV sequences.

Same variety as the c

audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant', final primary stress (rule 01 / 101, compounds excluded) rests on the 2021 ANU reference grammar, the best available and instrumentally supported description; the deciding quotation was verified verbatim at sec. 6.4.1 p. 241 with the schemata at sec. 5.5.4 p. 207 in the PDF downloaded this compilation. The grammar itself disposes of the only competing claims (Simon 1979 and Blench draft on tone). No better source exists; nothing to add beyond registering the now-copies we hold and page numbers (207, 241) in the record and setting an strength of the evidence (record 'grade' field is empty; the compilers had 'typeset-pdf').

sources.citation: Weedall 2021, A grammar of West Kameng Sajolang (Miji), ANU PhD, secs. 5.5.4 and 6.4 read from full thesis text; compounds excluded (stress by lexeme headedness), realized as pitch accent, no tone
sources.quote: Two-syllable words which are not compounds always have an initial unstressed syllable and a final stressed syllable. Three-syllable words which are not compounds always have an initial secondarily stressed syllable, a penultimate unstressed syllable, and a final primarily stressed syllable.
